source.title: Sparse CLIP: Co-Optimizing Interpretability and Performance in Contrastive Learning
source.authors: Chuan Qin; Constantin Venhoff; Sonia Joseph; Fanyi Xiao; Stefan Scherer

record.tranche_reason: The paper tests native sparse representations in CLIP, including their sparsity, multimodality and evolution, but does not test superposition geometry, capacity-driven polysemanticity, SAE feature completeness, or one-dimensional feature directions as described by the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper cites Toy Models of Superposition in its references but reports no results testing that work's claims. Its own results concern sparse CLIP representations, a related but different construct. The CLIP performance benchmarks and steering results do not measure the claim versions.
record.test_reason: The paper trains CLIP models built to be sparse (ReLU plus a 72x wider projection) and reports their benchmark scores, sparsity, multimodality and how features change over training. It cites Toy Models of Superposition only as background. It does not measure superposition geometry, capacity-driven polysemanticity, other causes of polysemanticity, LLM feature spread or SAE recovery, or feature dimensionality. The sparsity is induced on purpose by the architecture, so it is not observed arising on its own. The Prisma SAE comparison (Table 1, 1–2% zero-shot loss from imperfect reconstruction) is a comparison against the study's own method in a vision model. It does not test whether SAE features are complete, stable or canonical units. The record's relation 'tests' contradicts its own T6 tranche and all-'none' rows.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that training CLIP with ReLU and dimension expansion gives sparse, interpretable, mostly multimodal features with no loss in accuracy. They say this challenges the view that interpretability and performance trade off. They also report that feature concepts emerge early and can transform during training. They leave open whether the gains come from the added parameters (14% more in the vision tower) rather than from sparsity.
record.recipe_differences: The paper trains sparse CLIP models using high-dimensional projection and a ReLU constraint; it does not reproduce or apply the Toy Models of Superposition method.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that sparsity varies with embedding dimensionality and logit scale cap, and that lowering the cap to 20 substantially reduces zero-shot performance.

fits_no_version.finding: Sparse CLIP embeddings reach average L0 of 281–469 on 55,296 dimensions. Their Clarity scores beat open-weight CLIP SAEs (Table 3a).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Contrastive training with non-negativity and dimension expansion yields sparse, interpretable embeddings comparable to or clearer than post-hoc SAE features.

fits_no_version.finding: Features of the sparse CLIP are mostly multimodal, already at 1% of training. Individual feature concepts shift during training (e.g. goatee to Ryan Gosling to David Beckham).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Natively sparse multimodal features emerge early, and their semantics can be reassigned during training.

fits_no_version.finding: Reconstructed Prisma SAE features lose about 1–2% zero-shot accuracy versus the dense OpenAI ViT-B/32 (e.g. ImageNet 68.8 vs 67.5, Table 1).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Post-hoc SAE reconstructions of CLIP vision features do not fully preserve downstream performance.

record.problems: The study's findings concern CLIP variants trained for native sparsity, not the superposition claim versions. The paper notes that the projection adds 14% of parameters to the ViT-L/14 vision tower and that whether performance gains come from added parameters rather than sparsity remains open. No uncertainty estimates are stated for the reported results.
record.rows_left_out: Zero-shot classification, retrieval, VLM benchmark, and steering results were left out because they do not measure the claim versions or the sparse-feature findings recorded here.

untested.parts: No toy models, no sparsity-dependent transition, no geometry of overlapping directions.
No test of capacity competition or of important features getting dedicated dimensions.
No analysis of the causes of polysemantic neurons.
No LLM analysis. Sparsity in CLIP is imposed by architecture, not recovered from a dense model.
SAE completeness, stability and canonicity are not tested. SAE features appear only as a performance baseline (Prisma, Table 1; Table 3a).

record.verdict_notes: The record's relation 'tests' conflicts with its tranche T6 and with every row linked to 'none'; corrected to cites_only. Rows R1–R4 report the study's own method's sparsity (L0), which is a selection or design outcome rather than a test of any version.

versions.untested_parts: Toy-network superposition geometry, sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular geometric arrangements.
Whether limited capacity causes neuron polysemanticity or allocates dedicated dimensions to important features.
Whether polysemantic neurons arise through mechanisms other than capacity pressure.
Feature distributions in LLMs and recovery of LLM features with dictionaries or SAEs.
Whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units of a model's representation.
Whether superposed features are one-dimensional directions rather than multidimensional features.

rows.measure: Whether features activate for both image and text inputs
rows.value: The text says most features activate for both modalities from very early training, and that the 1% modality distribution closely resembles the final distribution.
rows.note: The figures show the distributions; the text describes the main pattern but gives no numeric proportions.
rows.check: Multimodality of features in a CLIP trained to be sparse is not a claim version. The reading is figure-only, so the 'observed' state has no version to be judged against.

rows.subject: ViT-L/14 Sparse+
rows.operation_detail: Tracked top-activated words and images for selected features over training.

conditions.value: multiple stages; exact stage-specific values not stated

rows.value: The feature initially activated for red fruits and random creatures, narrowed to rose hips mid-training, and later became a dog rose detector that retained hip activations.
rows.note: A qualitative trajectory in native Sparse CLIP features; it does not establish instability or incompleteness of SAE features.
rows.check: A qualitative feature trajectory across training checkpoints of a model built for sparsity. It does not show SAE feature stability or canonicity (V5). The state relative to any version cannot be set.
